FARRA:v3p242/r5.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p242/r5.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p242/r5.claim: The morning breathes when daylight has risen.

TAB-FULL:v24p163/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p163/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p163/r1.claim: The oath is by daylight as its brightness arrives and becomes clear.

TAB-FULL:v24p163/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p163/r2.speaker: سعيد
TAB-FULL:v24p163/r2.claim: Saʿīd says dawn has risen or emerged.

TAB-FULL:v24p163/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p163/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v24p163/r3.claim: Qatāda says dawn brightens and comes on.

ZAJJAJ:v5p291/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p291/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p291/r4.claim: The dawn “breathes” when it spreads until daylight is clear.

NAHHAS:v5p161/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p161/r1.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p161/r1.claim: The dawn shines and comes forward.

THALABI:v10p141/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p141/r9.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p141/r9.claim: The morning's breathing means its arrival and brightening, the first appearance of daylight, or its spreading and rising.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p217/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p217/r4.speaker: علي وقتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p217/r4.claim: The breathing dawn means the appearance of first light.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p217/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p217/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p217/r6.claim: تنفس may mean that dawn's arrival becomes visible or that its light grows; a further possibility is that the day lengthens, as in the expression that the day has breathed.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r1.claim: The morning breathes when its light extends and spreads; daylight is said to breathe as it grows longer.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r2.speaker: ابن عباس والمفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r2.claim: They describe dawn rising, brightening, and spreading broadly across the sky.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r3.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r3.claim: He says dawn is breathing when daytime rises.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r4.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r4.claim: He says the breath is the morning extending until clear daylight.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r5.speaker: أبو عبيدة عن علقمة بن قرط
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r5.claim: A poetic line says dawn breathed and the night withdrew; it witnesses the expression for dawn spreading.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r6.speaker: الأزهري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p271/r6.claim: Tanffasa can mean split or cleave until something is clear, like a bow splitting; al-Lihyani calls a crack in an arrow or bow nafs.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:81:18-20/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:81:18-20/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:81:18-20/r2.claim: The dawn's breathing means its light extends until it becomes clear day.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p349/r12.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p349/r12.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p349/r12.claim: The morning breathes as its first light appears, or its brightness extends and rises.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p43/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p43/r1.speaker: أبو عبيدة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p43/r1.claim: Abū ʿUbayda cites the poet ʿAlqama ibn Qurṭ's line about dawn breathing, as evidence for the expression.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p43/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p43/r2.speaker: علي وقتادة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p43/r2.claim: The breathing dawn means the first appearance of dawn.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p43/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p43/r4.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p43/r4.claim: The phrase describes daylight stretching until it becomes clearly day.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p43/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p43/r5.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p43/r5.claim: The answer to this oath begins with the oath by the retreating stars in 81:15.

RAZI-FULL:v31p67/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p67/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p67/r1.claim: Some take asʿasa as the night coming on, paired with dawn's arrival; others take it as night retreating at the first light, followed by dawn becoming fully bright, like 74:33-34.

RAZI-FULL:v31p67/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p67/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p67/r2.claim: Dawn's breathing means that it brightens, as in 74:34.

RAZI-FULL:v31p67/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p67/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p67/r3.claim: One metaphor gives dawn a spirit and breeze as it arrives; another compares dark night to a grief-stricken person relieved by taking a breath when dawn comes.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:18-22/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:18-22/r1.speaker: أبو عمرو
QURTUBI-FULL:81:18-22/r1.claim: The verb taʿsaʿsa can mean to smell; he cites a wolf's muzzle as evidence, and it also means seeking game at night.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:18-22/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:18-22/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:81:18-22/r2.claim: The morning's breathing means its light expands until daylight becomes clear; people also say the day breathes when it grows.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:18-22/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:18-22/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:81:18-22/r3.claim: Breathing is the breeze's emergence from inside; alternatively, the morning splits open, as an archer's bow is said to breathe when it cracks.

BAYDAWI-FULL:81:15-21/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:81:15-21/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:81:15-21/r3.claim: The morning breathes when it brightens, its remaining darkness likened to the breeze and spirit of dawn.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p320#6/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p320#6/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p320#6/r1.claim: The dawn's light extends; because dawn brings air and breeze, its arrival is figuratively called breathing. It is the oath's answer.

QASHANI:81:18-19/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:81:18-19/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:81:18-19/r1.claim: Dawn is the effect of the rising spirit-sun, spreading through the body and granting it life.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p338/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p338/r1.speaker: الضحاك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p338/r1.claim: Al-Dahhak says the dawn breathes when it rises; Qatadah says it brightens and arrives, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr says it begins to emerge, as also transmitted from Ali.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p338/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p338/r2.speaker: ابن جرير
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p338/r2.claim: Ibn Jarir explains the oath as the light of daytime when it approaches and becomes clear.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p335#s081/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p335#s081/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p335#s081/r1.claim: Al-Takwīr threatens the climactic Day of Judgment and chastises Qur’an deniers; the Qur’an is a reminder in honored, pure pages delivered by trusted angels.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p335/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p335/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p335/r1.claim: Al-Takwīr threatens the Day of Judgment as the climactic display of divine majesty and warns those who reject the Qur’an, a reminder preserved in honored, pure pages by angelic scribes.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p340/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p340/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p340/r1.claim: The cosmic signs in al-Takwīr precede the flight from relatives in ʿAbasa, so the opening of this surah signals the Hour and answers when it will come.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p340/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p340/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p340/r2.claim: After associating disgrace with the verse about humanity’s ingratitude, Biqāʿī says the gravest denial after shirk is rejecting the truth, especially the Qur’an.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p341/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p341/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p341/r2.claim: The rhetorical ellipsis mentions the stars’ retreat and concealment to imply their appearance, then mentions night to imply the omitted day.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p341/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p341/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p341/r3.claim: The morning breathes by shining and spreading its gentle light, dispelling night after night has arrived and departed.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p341/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p341/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p341/r4.claim: Even dawn’s light and pleasure pale beside the Qur’an’s light and spiritual delight; the sun’s heat erases morning’s coolness, but nothing erases the Qur’an’s sacred refreshment.

DURR-FULL:v8p433/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p433/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p433/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says the night turns away and the morning breathes when daylight begins at dawn.

BURSEVI:v10p271/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p271/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p271/r8.claim: Tanaffasa describes dawn as breathing, meaning the beginning of its rise.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r1.claim: “Dawn breathing” means its brightening and spreading light. Al-Kashshaf explains it as dawn bringing a breeze and relief, with breath used metaphorically for the breeze.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes the arriving breeze as breath by metaphor; the phrase makes dawn itself breathe by an explicit metaphor with figurative attribution.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r3.speaker: الإمام
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r3.claim: Al-Razi compares the dark night to a distressed person relieved by breathing: dawn's emergence from darkness is release from distress into ease; Alusi calls this subtler than al-Kashshaf's account.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r4.claim: Another explanation likens night covering and burying day to death, with dawn's light appearing like the breath that signals life; another takes the word as the dawn widening into daytime.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r5.claim: The apparent reference is the true dawn, whose light spreads horizontally, distinguished from the false dawn's vertical column that fades or diminishes before the true dawn spreads.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r6.speaker: رسول الله
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r6.claim: A Muslim report warns that neither Bilal's call nor the vertical false-dawn glow should deceive people; they wait until dawn spreads across the horizon.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r7.claim: Alusi disputes an astronomical objection attributed to al-Razi: it overlooks the Earth's shadow and reflected rays reaching observers in different regions.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r8.claim: For the oath syntax, idha is not governed by the oath verb, since that would wrongly restrict the oath by time; it attaches instead to an omitted noun such as the greatness of night or day.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r9.speaker: عصام الدين
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#3/r9.claim: ʿIsam al-Din instead treats idha as a prospective circumstantial qualification of the object sworn by, making the oath about night as it comes to that time.

ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r5.claim: The morning’s breathing means the moment it starts to brighten, like 74:34, and also evokes the delicacy of the gentle morning breeze.

ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r6.claim: The dawn dispels the distress of night and promises the Prophet and Muslims a good outcome, as expressed in 93:4.

ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r7.claim: The believers’ present world is a night turning toward morning, and the Judgment when each soul learns what it prepared is like a breathing dawn.

TABATABAI:81:15-18/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:81:15-18/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:81:15-18/r7.claim: Dawn is described as breathing because its light spreads over the horizon and drives darkness away; a person resting after hard labor is the image, which the author finds more intuitive than Zamakhshari's spirit-and-breeze metaphor.

TABATABAI:81:15-18/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:81:15-18/r8.speaker: الزمخشري
TABATABAI:81:15-18/r8.claim: Zamakhshari says dawn's arrival brings a spirit and breeze, which are metaphorically its breath.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p194/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p194/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p194/r3.claim: The stars and the night-to-dawn transition testify that the Qur'an is not soothsayer chant but was brought by God's mighty, honored, obeyed, trustworthy angel.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p201/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p201/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p201/r3.claim: The oath passage refutes the disbelievers' claim that neither the Qur'an is revelation nor Muhammad is God's messenger; they spread this charge to blunt the Prophet's influence.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p202/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p202/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p202/r1.claim: Soothsayers claimed contact with jinn who disclosed the unseen, casting their rhymed utterances as revelation; the Qur'an rejects the idea that the Prophet is their kind.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p203/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p203/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p203/r3.claim: The prefixed lā in these oaths is not denial of the oath; it negates the addressees' claim being refuted by the oath.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p205/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p205/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p205/r4.claim: The retreating night and breathing dawn form another oath that supports the preceding claim about the Qur'an.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p206/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p206/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p206/r1.claim: The paired oaths substantiate the Hereafter as the premise under discussion.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p206/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p206/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p206/r2.claim: Tanffasa means dawn's appearance and pictures dawn gasping under night's weight until God lifts its covering.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:81:15/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:81:15/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:81:15/r1.claim: The elegant oaths in verses 15–18 confirm the coming claims about revelation and the Prophet and prepare listeners to grasp their importance; doubters would accept no religious message otherwise.

STUDYQURAN:81:18/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:81:18/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:81:18/r1.claim: Morning breathes as it seems to awaken from night and its light spreads like exhaled breath until day.

STUDYQURAN:81:18/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:81:18/r2.speaker: some
STUDYQURAN:81:18/r2.claim: If night approaches in verse 17, this verse refers to morning rising; if night recedes, it refers to morning's rise or gradual illumination.
